# The Smallest Positive That Is Missing — Explained, One Approach at a Time

<!-- Generated by scripts/gen-explained.mjs from src/data/problems/arrays-hashing/first-missing-positive.ts.
     Edit the data, then run `npm run docs:explained`. Edits here are overwritten. -->

**Arrays & Hashing** · hard · [the same question on LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/first-missing-positive/)

Given an unsorted integer array, return the smallest positive integer (1, 2, 3, …) that does not appear in it. Zeroes and negatives may be present but can never be the answer. The follow-up — and the whole difficulty — is doing it in linear time with only a constant amount of extra memory.

## What the input promises

- 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5
- -2^31 <= nums[i] <= 2^31 - 1 — zeroes, negatives and duplicates are all allowed
- the answer always lies in 1..n+1, because n values can cover at most n consecutive positives
- any value <= 0 or > n is noise: it can never be the answer and it never blocks one
- O(n) time AND O(1) extra space is the requirement — a hash set is a correct answer that fails the follow-up
- the input array may be modified; nothing promises it comes back intact

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `nums = [1, 2, 0]` | `3` | — |
| `nums = [3, 4, -1, 1]` | `2` | The answer is a hole in the middle, not one past the end — a solution that only extends the longest run misses it. |
| `nums = [7, 8, 9, 11, 12]` | `1` | Nothing in 1..n is present at all. Every value is noise and the answer is the very first candidate. |

<details>
<summary>Hints, one nudge at a time — open them in order</summary>

1. How large can the answer possibly be? With n values in hand, name the biggest answer you could ever be forced to give.
2. That bound means anything <= 0 or > n is irrelevant. The only interesting values are 1..n — exactly as many of them as the array has slots.
3. You are allowed to wreck the input. Put value v into slot v-1; afterwards the first slot that disagrees with its own index names the answer.

</details>

---

## 1. Try 1, then 2, then 3

Ask the array whether it holds 1; if it does, ask about 2, and so on. The first candidate that is absent is the answer, and n+1 candidates is always enough because the array cannot block more than n of them.

```python
def first_missing_positive(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    for c in range(1, len(nums) + 2):
        found = False
        for x in nums:
            if x == c:
                found = True
                break
        if not found:
            return c
    return len(nums) + 1
```

**O(n^2) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int firstMissingPositive(int[] nums) {
    for (int c = 1; c <= nums.length + 1; c++) {
        boolean found = false;
        for (int x : nums) {
            if (x == c) { found = true; break; }
        }
        if (!found) return c;
    }
    return nums.length + 1;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
int firstMissingPositive(vector<int> nums) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    for (int c = 1; c <= n + 1; c++) {
        bool found = false;
        for (int x : nums) {
            if (x == c) { found = true; break; }
        }
        if (!found) return c;
    }
    return n + 1;
}
```

</details>

## 2. Sort, then walk

> **Why now.** Rescanning the whole array once per candidate repeats the same comparisons endlessly: candidate 5 re-reads everything candidates 1 through 4 already read. Sorting arranges the values so one left-to-right walk settles every candidate at once.

Sort, then walk with a counter holding the next positive still wanted. Duplicates and values below the counter are skipped; the first value that overshoots proves the counter is missing.

```python
def first_missing_positive(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    nums.sort()
    want = 1
    for x in nums:
        if x == want:
            want += 1
        elif x > want:
            break
    return want
```

**O(n log n) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int firstMissingPositive(int[] nums) {
    Arrays.sort(nums);
    int want = 1;
    for (int x : nums) {
        if (x == want) want++;
        else if (x > want) break;
    }
    return want;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
int firstMissingPositive(vector<int> nums) {
    sort(nums.begin(), nums.end());
    int want = 1;
    for (int x : nums) {
        if (x == want) want++;
        else if (x > want) break;
    }
    return want;
}
```

</details>

## 3. Hash set

> **Why now.** The sort spends O(n log n) arranging values into an order the answer never asks about — it only ever asks whether one particular number is present. A set answers exactly that in constant time, so the ordering work was pure waste.

Pour every value into a set, then probe 1, 2, 3, … until a probe misses. Each probe is O(1), so the whole thing is linear.

```python
def first_missing_positive(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    seen = set(nums)
    want = 1
    while want in seen:
        want += 1
    return want
```

**O(n) time · O(n) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int firstMissingPositive(int[] nums) {
    Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
    for (int x : nums) seen.add(x);
    int want = 1;
    while (seen.contains(want)) want++;
    return want;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
int firstMissingPositive(vector<int> nums) {
    unordered_set<int> seen(nums.begin(), nums.end());
    int want = 1;
    while (seen.count(want)) want++;
    return want;
}
```

</details>

## 4. Boolean table of size n+1

> **Why now.** The set stores every value, including the negatives and the huge ones that can never be part of any answer, and it pays a hash on each insert and each probe. Once the answer is known to be capped at n+1, an array of n+1 flags indexes straight into itself — no hashing, and an out-of-range value is dropped the moment it is seen.

Because the answer lives in 1..n+1, only the values 1..n matter. Tick those off in a flat boolean array indexed by the value itself, then return the first index never ticked.

```python
def first_missing_positive(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    n = len(nums)
    seen = [False] * (n + 1)
    for x in nums:
        if 1 <= x <= n:
            seen[x] = True
    for c in range(1, n + 1):
        if not seen[c]:
            return c
    return n + 1
```

**O(n) time · O(n) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int firstMissingPositive(int[] nums) {
    int n = nums.length;
    boolean[] seen = new boolean[n + 1];
    for (int x : nums) {
        if (x >= 1 && x <= n) seen[x] = true;
    }
    for (int c = 1; c <= n; c++) {
        if (!seen[c]) return c;
    }
    return n + 1;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
int firstMissingPositive(vector<int> nums) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    vector<bool> seen(n + 1, false);
    for (int x : nums) {
        if (x >= 1 && x <= n) seen[x] = true;
    }
    for (int c = 1; c <= n; c++) {
        if (!seen[c]) return c;
    }
    return n + 1;
}
```

</details>

## 5. The one to remember

> **Why now.** The boolean table is linear in time but still allocates n+1 fresh cells, which is exactly what the O(1)-space follow-up forbids. The input array already has n slots, and nobody needs its original contents once the answer is out — so the marking table can BE the input: send each value v to slot v-1 and the array marks itself.

Two passes over the array itself. First, place every value that could matter: while nums[i] sits in 1..n and is not already in slot nums[i]-1, swap it there. The swap is the trick — the value that lands in position i is examined next, so every swap puts one value permanently home and the total number of swaps is at most n, which keeps the nested while loop linear. The guard nums[nums[i]-1] != nums[i] is what stops a duplicate from swapping with its twin forever. Second, walk the slots: the first i whose value is not i+1 means i+1 was never placed, so return i+1. If every slot is home, 1..n are all present and the answer is n+1.

```python
def first_missing_positive(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    n = len(nums)
    for i in range(n):
        # keep sending the value at i home until i holds junk or is settled
        while 1 <= nums[i] <= n and nums[nums[i] - 1] != nums[i]:
            j = nums[i] - 1
            nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]
    for i in range(n):
        if nums[i] != i + 1:
            return i + 1
    return n + 1
```

**O(n) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int firstMissingPositive(int[] nums) {
    int n = nums.length;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        while (nums[i] >= 1 && nums[i] <= n && nums[nums[i] - 1] != nums[i]) {
            int j = nums[i] - 1;
            int t = nums[j];
            nums[j] = nums[i];
            nums[i] = t;
        }
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (nums[i] != i + 1) return i + 1;
    }
    return n + 1;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
int firstMissingPositive(vector<int> nums) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        while (nums[i] >= 1 && nums[i] <= n && nums[nums[i] - 1] != nums[i]) {
            int j = nums[i] - 1;
            int t = nums[j];
            nums[j] = nums[i];
            nums[i] = t;
        }
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (nums[i] != i + 1) return i + 1;
    }
    return n + 1;
}
```

</details>

## The arc

| # | Approach | Cost | What it adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Try 1, then 2, then 3 | O(n^2) time · O(1) space | the baseline — nothing before it |
| 2 | Sort, then walk | O(n log n) time · O(1) space | Rescanning the whole array once per candidate repeats the same comparisons endlessly: candidate 5 re-reads everything candidates 1 through 4 already read. Sorting arranges the values so one left-to-right walk settles every candidate at once. |
| 3 | Hash set | O(n) time · O(n) space | The sort spends O(n log n) arranging values into an order the answer never asks about — it only ever asks whether one particular number is present. A set answers exactly that in constant time, so the ordering work was pure waste. |
| 4 | Boolean table of size n+1 | O(n) time · O(n) space | The set stores every value, including the negatives and the huge ones that can never be part of any answer, and it pays a hash on each insert and each probe. Once the answer is known to be capped at n+1, an array of n+1 flags indexes straight into itself — no hashing, and an out-of-range value is dropped the moment it is seen. |
| 5 | The one to remember | O(n) time · O(1) space | The boolean table is linear in time but still allocates n+1 fresh cells, which is exactly what the O(1)-space follow-up forbids. The input array already has n slots, and nobody needs its original contents once the answer is out — so the marking table can BE the input: send each value v to slot v-1 and the array marks itself. |

## Full runnable script

Every rung in one file, printed against the inputs `npm run verify:run`
drives the Java and C++ blocks with. Run it: `python explained.py`.

```python
def first_missing_positive_try_1_then_2_then_3(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    for c in range(1, len(nums) + 2):
        found = False
        for x in nums:
            if x == c:
                found = True
                break
        if not found:
            return c
    return len(nums) + 1


def first_missing_positive_sort_then_walk(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    nums.sort()
    want = 1
    for x in nums:
        if x == want:
            want += 1
        elif x > want:
            break
    return want


def first_missing_positive_hash_set(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    seen = set(nums)
    want = 1
    while want in seen:
        want += 1
    return want


def first_missing_positive_boolean_table_of_size_n_1(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    n = len(nums)
    seen = [False] * (n + 1)
    for x in nums:
        if 1 <= x <= n:
            seen[x] = True
    for c in range(1, n + 1):
        if not seen[c]:
            return c
    return n + 1


def first_missing_positive_the_one_to_remember(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    n = len(nums)
    for i in range(n):
        # keep sending the value at i home until i holds junk or is settled
        while 1 <= nums[i] <= n and nums[nums[i] - 1] != nums[i]:
            j = nums[i] - 1
            nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]
    for i in range(n):
        if nums[i] != i + 1:
            return i + 1
    return n + 1

APPROACHES = [
    first_missing_positive_try_1_then_2_then_3,
    first_missing_positive_sort_then_walk,
    first_missing_positive_hash_set,
    first_missing_positive_boolean_table_of_size_n_1,
    first_missing_positive_the_one_to_remember,
]

# the same inputs npm run verify:run drives the Java and C++ blocks with:
# an answer that is not adjacent to any value present — [7,8,9,11,12] answers 1 with nothing in range, and [2,2,2] is the duplicate that makes an unguarded index-swap spin forever
CASES = [
    lambda: ([1,2,0],),
    lambda: ([3,4,-1,1],),
    lambda: ([7,8,9,11,12],),
    lambda: ([1],),
    lambda: ([2,2,2],),
    lambda: ([-5],),
    lambda: ([2,1],),
    lambda: ([2,2,1],),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for fn in APPROACHES:
        answers = []
        for make in CASES:
            try:
                answers.append(fn(*make()))
            except BaseException as exc:  # a rung that raises names itself
                answers.append(f"!{exc}")
        print(f"{fn.__name__:<50} -> {answers}")
```
